notes:
Mean deviation

  • About the mean: $MD_{\bar x}=\dfrac1n\sum|x_i-\bar x|$ (ungrouped); for frequency data $MD_{\bar x}=\dfrac1N\sum f_i|x_i-\bar x|$, $N=\sum f_i$.
  • About the median: same formula with $\bar x$ replaced by the median. Mean deviation is always computed using absolute (unsigned) deviations, since signed deviations from the mean always sum to zero.

Variance and standard deviation

  • Ungrouped data: $\sigma^2=\dfrac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$; $\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}$.
  • Frequency data: $\sigma^2=\dfrac1N\sum f_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$.
  • Shortcut formula: $\sigma^2=\dfrac1N\sum f_ix_i^2-\bar x^2$.
  • Step-deviation method (class width $h$, $u_i=\frac{x_i-A}{h}$): $\sigma^2=h^2\left[\dfrac{\sum f_iu_i^2}{N}-\left(\dfrac{\sum f_iu_i}{N}\right)^2\right]$.
  • Standard deviation of the first $n$ natural numbers: $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}}$.

Effect of change of origin and scale

TransformationEffect on variance/SD
Add/subtract a constant $a$unchanged (independent of change of origin)
Multiply by a constant $k$variance $\times k^2$; SD $\times|k|$ (depends on change of scale)

Coefficient of variation

  • $CV=\dfrac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%$. The series with the smaller CV is more consistent (less variable).

Key facts

  • Variance (and hence SD) is always non-negative; it is 0 only when all observations are equal.
  • Mean deviation about the mean is always $\le$ the standard deviation.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 1-2 questions from this chapter — computing mean deviation/variance/SD for a small ungrouped data set, or a conceptual question on how variance changes under a shift or scaling of the data. Remember: shifting data does not change variance; scaling by $k$ multiplies variance by $k^2$.

questions.explanation: Mean $=6$; squared deviations $16,4,0,4,16$ sum to $40$; variance $=40/5=8$; $\sigma=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$.

questions.q: A data set has mean 25 and standard deviation 5. Its coefficient of variation is
questions.explanation: $CV=\dfrac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100=\dfrac{5}{25}\times100=20\%$.

questions.q: The mean deviation about the median of $4,7,10$ is
questions.explanation: Median $=7$; deviations $3,0,3$ sum to $6$; $MD=6/3=2$.

questions.q: The variance of any data set is
options: can be negative for small samples
non-negative, and zero only when all observations are equal
questions.explanation: Variance is a sum of squares divided by $n$, so it can never be negative; it equals zero only when every observation equals the mean.

questions.q: If every observation of a data set is increased by 5, the variance
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by the same amount, so the deviations from the mean — and hence the variance — do not change.

questions.q: If every observation of a data set is multiplied by 3, the variance
questions.explanation: Multiplying each value by $k$ multiplies every deviation by $k$, so variance (a squared quantity) scales by $k^2=9$.

questions.q: The standard deviation of the first 7 natural numbers is
questions.explanation: $\sigma=\sqrt{\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{49-1}{12}}=\sqrt4=2$.

questions.q: For 5 observations with mean 10, the sum of squared deviations from the mean is 50. The standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Variance $=\dfrac{50}{5}=10$, so $\sigma=\sqrt{10}$.

questions.q: Series A has mean 50 and SD 5; series B has mean 60 and SD 9. Which series is more consistent?
questions.explanation: $CV_A=\dfrac5{50}\times100=10\%$, $CV_B=\dfrac9{60}\times100=15\%$. Lower CV means more consistent, so A is more consistent.

questions.q: Mean deviation (about the mean or median) is always computed using
questions.explanation: Signed deviations from the mean always sum to zero, so mean deviation uses $|x_i-\bar x|$ or $|x_i-\text{median}|$ instead.

questions.q: The variance of the data $7,7,7,7,7$ is
questions.explanation: All values equal the mean, so every deviation is 0 and the variance is 0.

questions.q: If the variance of a data set is 16, its standard deviation is
questions.explanation: $\sigma=\sqrt{\text{variance}}=\sqrt{16}=4$.

questions.q: The mean and variance of 6 observations are 8 and 16. If 4 is added to each observation, the new mean and variance are
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts the mean by that constant (new mean $=8+4=12$) but leaves the variance unchanged (still 16).

questions.q: The mean deviation about the mean of a data set is
options: always greater than its standard deviation
always less than or equal to its standard deviation
always equal to its standard deviation
questions.explanation: It is a standard result that mean deviation about the mean never exceeds the standard deviation of the same data.

questions.q: Standard deviation is independent of
questions.explanation: Shifting all values by a constant (change of origin) does not affect SD, but multiplying by a constant (change of scale) does.

questions.q: A data set has variance 25. If every observation is divided by 5, the new variance is
questions.explanation: Dividing by a constant $k$ scales variance by $k^2$: $25\times(1/5)^2=25/25=1$.

Data set A has mean 40, SD 8; data set B has mean 50, SD 8. Which is relatively more variable?
questions.explanation: $CV_A=\dfrac8{40}\times100=20\%$, $CV_B=\dfrac8{50}\times100=16\%$. The higher CV (A) means A is relatively more variable.

questions.q: The variance of a data set is measured in
options: the square of the units of the data
the reciprocal of the units of the data
the same units as the data
questions.explanation: Since variance is an average of squared deviations, its units are the square of the original data's units (SD restores the original units).

questions.q: A data set of 9 observations has mean 20 and variance 9. The sum of squared deviations from the mean is
questions.explanation: $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}{n} \Rightarrow 9=\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}{9} \Rightarrow \sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=81$.

questions.q: A distribution has SD 5. If every value is increased by 20% (multiplied by 1.2), the new SD is
questions.explanation: SD scales by the same multiplicative factor as the data: $5\times1.2=6$.

questions.q: The mean of 10 observations is 10. It is later found that an observation 3 was wrongly recorded instead of the correct value 8. The corrected mean is
questions.explanation: Original sum $=100$. Corrected sum $=100-3+8=105$; corrected mean $=105/10=10.5$.

questions.q: The standard deviation of a data set can never be
questions.explanation: SD is the non-negative square root of variance, so it can never be negative.

questions.explanation: Adding a constant to every observation shifts the mean equally, leaving all deviations — and hence the variance — unchanged.

questions.q: If the variance of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ is $\sigma^2$, the variance of $2x_1,\ldots,2x_n$ is
questions.explanation: Multiplying every observation by $k$ multiplies variance by $k^2$; here $k=2$, so the new variance is $4\sigma^2$.

questions.q: Which measure of dispersion is based only on the two extreme observations of a data set?
questions.explanation: Range $=$ maximum value $-$ minimum value, using only the two extreme observations, unlike MD/variance/SD which use every observation.

questions.q: The shortcut (computational) formula for variance of ungrouped data is
questions.explanation: Variance equals the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean: $\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2$.

questions.q: A data set of 6 values has mean 9. If its standard deviation is 0, then
questions.explanation: SD $=0$ means every deviation from the mean is 0, so every observation must equal the mean, 9.

questions.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 6. After removing one number, the mean of the remaining 4 numbers becomes 5. The removed number is
questions.explanation: Sum of 5 numbers $=30$; sum of remaining 4 $=20$; removed number $=30-20=10$.

questions.q: The coefficient of variation is mainly used to compare
options: only the absolute spread of one data set
the relative variability of two or more data sets
the central tendency of two data sets
questions.explanation: CV expresses SD as a percentage of the mean, allowing fair comparison of variability between data sets with different units or means.
